hook.support: Your mate says energy drinks are fine every day. Is that true? How do they know? Good advice has proof. And you say where the proof came from.
hook.core: “Trust me, bro” isn’t evidence. When you give advice at work, in a talk or online, people want to know: how do you know that? Good advice is backed by facts from sources people can trust, and you give credit to whoever did the work.
hook.extend: Advice is only as strong as its evidence. To present it well, find reliable support and say where it came from. And respect copyright when you use other people’s words, images or music.

why.support: Proof makes people trust your advice. Giving credit is fair and it’s the law.
why.core: Backing your advice with evidence makes people trust you. Crediting sources keeps you honest, and keeps you out of trouble.
why.extend: Workplaces, courses and public life all expect evidence and credit. Breaking copyright can cost money and trust.

articles.title: How do you know?

body.support:
Advice is better with **evidence**. Evidence is a fact that shows you’re right.

**Find a good source.** A **source** is where a fact comes from. Ask:
- Who wrote it?
- Do they know about this?
- Is it new?
- Are they trying to sell me something?
.
**Good sources** include government websites, experts and trusted news.

**Give credit.** When you use a fact, say where it came from.
- When you speak: “The Cancer Council says…”.
- When you write: put the source in a **reference list** at the end.
.
**Copyright.** Songs, photos and videos belong to the person who made them. That’s called **copyright**. You can’t just use them.
- Ask first.
- Or use free ones that say you can.
- Always say who made it.
body.core:
Good advice answers the question everyone’s thinking: *how do you know?*

**1. Find evidence.** **Evidence** includes facts, numbers, expert advice and real examples. One strong piece beats five weak ones.

**2. Check the source is reliable.** A **reliable** source is one you can trust. Ask:
- **Who** made it? An expert, a government agency, a trusted organisation?
- **When?** Is it up to date?
- **Why?** Is it trying to inform you, or sell to you?
- **Can you check it** somewhere else?
.
**3. Give credit when you speak.** This is called **attribution**. It also makes your advice sound stronger.
- “According to the Bureau of Meteorology…”.
- “A 2024 report by the ABS found…”.
- “Dr Smith, a sleep expert, says…”.

**4. List your sources.** A **reference list** at the end of slides or a handout. A simple format:
- **Who.** (**Year**). *Title*. **Website**. Link.
- Example: Cancer Council Australia. (2024). *Slip, Slop, Slap, Seek, Slide*. cancer.org.au.

**5. Respect copyright.** **Copyright** protects songs, images, videos and writing. It belongs to the creator, even if it’s online and free to view.
- Use your own photos and music, or.
- use content with a licence that allows it, and credit the creator, or.
- ask permission.
.
Putting someone’s song in your video without permission can break copyright law.
body.extend:
Advice gets its strength from **evidence**: data, expert views, research and real examples. To present it well, choose **reliable** evidence and make clear where it came from.

**Evaluating sources.** Consider:
- **authority:** who created it, and what expertise they have.
- **currency:** how recent it is.
- **purpose:** to inform, persuade or sell.
- **corroboration:** whether other reliable sources agree.

**Attribution in speech.** Spoken **attribution** shows you are honest and well informed: “According to…”, “Research from… shows…”. Name the source before the claim, so listeners can judge it.

**Referencing in writing.** A **reference list** gives readers enough to find each source. A simple author–date format:
- **Author or organisation. (Year). *Title*. Publisher or website. URL**.

Be consistent, list sources in alphabetical order, and include everything you quoted or used.

**Copyright principles.** In Australia, **copyright** is automatic. Creators don’t need to register it. It covers text, images, music, film and software. It usually lasts 70 years after the creator dies. Being able to view something online does not mean you can reuse it.

Your options:
- create your own material.
- use material under a licence such as **Creative Commons**, following its conditions (usually attribution).
- seek permission.
- rely on limited exceptions, such as some uses for study, criticism or review.

Attribution is required in most cases. But crediting a creator does not, by itself, give you permission to use their work.

caseStudies.title: The kookaburra and the flute

body.support:
**Kookaburra Sits in the Old Gum Tree** is a kids’ song. A teacher named **Marion Sinclair** wrote it in **1934**.

In the 1980s, the band **Men at Work** had a huge hit called **Down Under**. It has a flute part.

Years later, people noticed the flute part sounded like the kookaburra song.

The company that owned the kookaburra song took the band’s record company to court. In **2010**, the court agreed. The flute part copied a big part of the song.

The owners got **5%** of the money the song makes from then on.

The lesson: even a short tune belongs to someone. Give credit, and ask first.
body.core:
**Kookaburra Sits in the Old Gum Tree** was written in **1934** by **Marion Sinclair**, a teacher. Later, the copyright was owned by a company called **Larrikin Music**.

In the early 1980s, **Men at Work** had a worldwide hit with **Down Under**. Its famous flute part included a few bars that sounded like the kookaburra song.

Larrikin took legal action against the record company and the songwriters. In **February 2010**, the Federal Court found that **Down Under** had copied a **substantial part** of the kookaburra song. That broke copyright.

Larrikin had asked for a large share of the song’s royalties. The court gave it **5%**.

The band appealed and lost in **2011**.

It was only a few bars of a kids’ song. But copyright still applied, decades later.
body.extend:
**Kookaburra Sits in the Old Gum Tree** was written in **1934** by **Marion Sinclair**. The copyright was later held by **Larrikin Music**.

Men at Work’s **Down Under** became an international hit in the early 1980s. Its flute riff included a short phrase resembling the kookaburra round.

Larrikin sued the record company and songwriters. In **February 2010**, the Federal Court found that **Down Under** reproduced a **substantial part** of Kookaburra, infringing copyright. The judge stressed that this did not mean the riff was the “hook” of Down Under.

Larrikin had sought up to 60% of royalties. In July 2010, the court awarded **5%** of the income from Down Under. An appeal was dismissed in **2011**.

The case shows several copyright principles at work. Protection lasts long after creation. A small part can still be “substantial” if it is an important part of the original. And familiarity, such as a song everyone learned at school, doesn’t make a work free to use.

It’s also a reminder that attribution and permission are different things. Using someone else’s work needs a legal basis, not just good intentions.

teacher.overview: Students learn to back advice with reliable evidence (checking who, when, why and whether others agree), give spoken attribution (“According to…”), write a simple reference list, and apply copyright basics (automatic protection, free to view is not free to use, licences, permission). They give one to two minutes of spoken advice with two credited sources. The case study is the Kookaburra / Down Under case (Federal Court, 2010), where a few bars of a 1934 children’s song were found to be a substantial part, and the owner was awarded 5% of royalties.
prep: Show students how to filter image searches by licence, or use free image libraries.
Optional: play both songs so students can hear the similarity.
Agree on a simple reference format for your school.

teacher.answers:
**Annotation:** 1 advice; 2 evidence; 3 spoken attribution; 4 image; 5 image credit (own photo); 6 reference (who, year, title, where).

**Sort:** needs credit or permission — ABS fact (credit); Google image (check licence or ask); hit song (permission or licence); expert quote (credit). No credit needed — your own photo; your own opinion.

**Case study:** in 2010 the Federal Court found Down Under reproduced a substantial part of Kookaburra (1934, Marion Sinclair; copyright held by Larrikin Music); 5% of royalties awarded; appeal dismissed in 2011. A small but important part can be substantial.

**Note:** check any facts in the sleep diagram and sunscreen model against current Sleep Health Foundation, Cancer Council and Bureau of Meteorology advice before teaching.

realityCheck: **Students will want to use music in videos.** Point them to royalty-free libraries; this is where the lesson becomes real.
**Referencing formats vary.** Keep it simple and consistent; who, year, title, where is enough at this level.
**Check the facts in the examples** (sleep hours, UV advice) against current sources before teaching.
**Works in a real class:** yes. Playing both songs side by side is a great hook.
